Allow the app to come and go, not just become ready once

For both the Lab app and ipywidgets use cases, we need to continuously
monitor whether the app is available: it might crash, or the user might
do something weird to its iframe, or they might simply close its window.
So we can't just have a one-time "ready" signal: we need events
indicating when the app is responding and when it isn't.

The UX here is somewhat poor: when the app isn't responding, instead
of raising an exception with a wonky stack trace, we should yield
a terse error message telling the user what to do.

Proper handling of coming-and-going of the app also exposes how we need
to have a way for pywwt to fully synchronize its internal state with the
state of the app. Right now, if you're using JupyterLab and connect a
second client to the app, it will reset the foreground/background
imagery. That's not desirable.

We also-also need a way to signal the client that the engine's internal
state has been reset so that references to, e.g. annotations and
data-table layers have been invalidated.

pywwt/tests/data/refimg_qt_full_step4: update for improved SFD map

I recently updated the `builtin-image-sets.wtml` file to match the
`imagesets6.xml` managed through the new-ish `wwt-core-catalogs`
repository. I created `builtin-image-sets.wtml` back when we couldn't
maintain the WWT servers in any reasonable way, so there was no
mechanism to update the imageset list. Now we have much better systems
for that and the `imagesets6` file was the one that was more recently
maintained.

Anyway, as part of that maintenance, the builtin SFD map switched from
the virtualearth.net data source to the WWT tiles.aspx data source. And
it turns out that they are slightly rotated relative to one another!
Fortunately, the new version (tiles.aspx) is more correct. The imagery
that we were using in our tests up until now used the older version, so
we need to update the reference images here.

Unrelated to this change, but it looks like we should check out the
other datasets that are served off of virtualearth.net and see whether
any of them also have astrometric issues.

lib/wwt.js: defensive coding for multiple views of a single model

In the Jupyter widget system, it is possible to create multiple views of a
single widget model. Views can be "detached", in which case their underlying
DOM elements are removed from the document. This is what happens if you create
a WWT view in a JupyterLab notebook, use the "Create a new view for this
output" context menu item to move the output to a new tab, and then hide the
original output. There is one underlying widget model and two views, only one
of which has active DOM elements.

The wrinkle for pywwt is that all of our widget state is stored inside the
<iframe> that does the rendering, so we're not really a real model-view setup.
The way things currently work, operations that affect the widget state are
passed as message from Python to JS, which are then distributed to all of the
views. So long as all views receive the same messages, things should stay in
sync. (Although if you create a widget, do some things to it, and then create
a new view of it, that view will have missed historical messages and so will
be out of sync.)

The problem I discovered was that if you send messages to a "detached" widget
view, you sometimes get JS exceptions. And apparently the code that
distributes the messages just terminates, preventing the control messages from
being sent to other widget views. This means that those views basically stop
responding to any Python controls.

This is bad news for the workflow of creating a WWT view then moving it to a
separate tab, which is something we very much want to support for UX reasons.
The real solution is to Do The Right Thing when a widget is detached, so that
the JS exceptions don't happen in the first place, but that's going to take
some time to get right. In the meantime, let's just log and swallow those JS
exceptions, so that the message passing can keep on working to the views that
aren't broken. This will keep things limping along.

pywwt/jupyter_server.py: add a separate static-file handler

This is to ease migration as we start switching to the WWT Kernel Data
Relay for hosting kernel data files.

There is still a value in having pywwt act as a Jupyter *server*
extension (which it does in addition to being a *notebook* extension and
a *JupyterLab* extension). This is because some Jupyter(Lab) setups deny
all cross-origin requests, which means that we have to host a local copy
of the research app for it to load any data from the kernel. Since pywwt
already bundles the research app, it's a natural place to do that, and
will remain so even if everyone uses the KDR, because it can host that
local copy even if no kernels are running. But to prevent clashes
between older and newer versions, we want to use a separate URL
namespace. So here we add support for serving files out of
`$baseurl/wwtstatic/`. For the time being, this is redundant with the
`/wwt/` code, but that should go away once we switch over to relying on
the KDR.

This change should get the lab app working better on platforms like
SciServer with cross-origin restrictions. There may still be some
issues, though, if the kernels and servers don't share home directories,
due to the way that the non-KDR service code works. At a minimum the KDR
rollout will still be important to enable the service of locally tiled
datasets.

Port the ipywidgets frontend to use the research app

Here we start using the research app for the ipywidgets Jupyter
frontend. This requires an extensive rework of the `frontend` JavaScript
package to adapt to the app messaging framework, which in turn required
a bunch of improvements to the app's messaging scheme to support the
ipywidgets use case. In particular, one ipywidgets "widget" might
include several "views", each of which is represented by an app, and the
message-passing infrastructure will receive messages from all active
apps at once. So we need to throw in various unique IDs that allow
everyone to keep track of which messages are meant for them.

This work is not complete. The JupyterLab app interface needs to be
updated to track some of the changes that were needed for the ipywidgets
frontend, and there are plenty of corner cases left dealing with cases
where widget views go away or stop being responsive. On the Python side,
we should pay attention to when there's actually a running app and when
it goes away, and raise exceptions as needed.

All that being said, this ought to get us going here, and I'd like to
get this baseline committed before starting to chase down issues like
the ones mentioned above.

Minimize JS<=>Python trait traffic with the WWT clock

Instead of sending out trait updates whenever the WWT clock changes,
update the client with the WWT clock, its rate, and a system reference
time more rarely. The client extrapolates the WWT clock time based on
those parameters. This allows us to get good-enough time readouts
without needing constant updates.

Because the Python code needs to receive new information from the
JavaScript frontend package, we'll need to make a new release of the JS
package and update the Python to require the new release. It's not a
breaking change in the JS since we still broadcast the engine time under
the same attribute name, even though you could think of it as breaking
since the rate of clock updates is now 600 times lower.

Bundle the research app in the pywwt distribution

Here we (ab)use the pywwt JS frontend package to distribute the WWT
research app in the pywwt `web_static` folder. We're not fully wired up
to use it everywhere yet, but this sets the stage for making it
available.

While the JupyterLab integration currently runs the research app from
its `wwtassets.org` origin, there are valid reasons to want to run a
local version. In particular, in the SciServer science platform the WWT
engine was unable to view FITS data because their system has some extra
security layers that block cross-origin requests to its Jupyter server
no matter what we try.

On the other hand, installations running the research app from an
official WWT domain will automatically pick up app upgrades, and if/when
we have user logins with interesting functionality (e.g. "save this
image to my account"), users will be able to take advantage of that
functionality.

much more robust, flexible, and extensible than the bundled server
extension, and it makes it possible for us to correctly expose tiled
data to WWT and other clients.

Rework image-testing approach

For the image-output testing suite, we used to have a library of
reference images for each platform and some complex logic to figure out
which image library to use depending on various OS and OpenGL
parameters. This turned out to be pretty annoying to manage since it
doesn't encourage re-use of reference images: if there's one specific
renderer setup that requires a special reference image for one case, you
have to set up a whole image library for that one setup.

Here we switch to just have a collection of reference images for each
test case. The test suite passes if *any* of these reference images
matches the observed output. This simplifies things a lot and makes
reuse much easier.

Major database schema updates: new tables for filters, mwcs, stretching, wct params (#395)

**Many to many relationships between different steps through association tables**
By far the biggest change: New individual tables for mwcs/stretching/wct params and mwcs_dtt/wct_dtt params. For mwcs/stretching/wct params it is now possible to define many different parameter choices and point them to one or many filters. Similarly many mwcs_dtt/wct_dtt_params can be defined and pointed to many mwcs/stretching/wct params. The relationships between different levels/steps is stored in association tables, and displayed dynamically in msnoise admin. For updating/inserting via api, a list of ids is used to update the association tables (e.g. defining which filter_ids a particular set of dvv params should point to).

When saving results, the convention follows filt_id/level1_id/level2_id.... where mwcs/stretching/wct_params are level one, and dtt params are level 2. Note, no intermediate wavelet transform results are saved (prior to dt/t) as the size of such files would be huge (i checked ;) ). So the wavelet transform + dt/t are still performed in one step for now... however its still now possible to have many to many relationship between different wavelet params and wavelet_dtt params.

Fix use of tables prefix in database creation

msnoise_table_def.py was defining the table names and reading the prefix
from the db.ini file at compilation time, right after the interpreter
starts (as the code was at module level, in the class declaration).

As a consequence, on a new project (with no db.ini file), the prefix
chosen by the user was added to the db.ini file but ignored when
creating the tables, which were always created without any prefix. When
re-initialising the database (when a db.ini already exists), only the
prefix written in db.ini during the last run of 'msnoise db init' was
used, and again, the prefix entered by the user was ignored and simply
stored in db.ini.

As SQLAlchemy Declarative system sets up the classes mapped to
relational database tables as soon as they are defined, this definition
has to be postponed to run-time to allow the table names to use a prefix
entered by the user.

The changes introduced by this commit move the definition of the mapped
classes to a function to allow the use of a prefix entered before by the
user (when initialising a new database) or read from the db.ini file
(when using an existing database).

Modules using these mapped classes are updated to call the function
defining the mapped class instead of directly importing the classes.

Additionally, the s000installer.py file is reworked for better
readability and maintainability:

 - indices are created in their own function

 - user input for database and password choice somewhat improved

 - improved readability and maintainability of code handling default
   values in user choices

 - for security, no default password is provided (to avoid weak default
   installation)

Better handling of a missing db.ini

As the db.ini is looked up through api.connect() very early at runtime,
even before any provided subcommand is even taken into account, db.ini
can legitimately not exist (as it is the case when running 'msnoise db
init').  api.read_database_inifile() should therefore not do a
sys.exit() when the file is not found, as an exit is not always wanted.

This was previously resolved by a very broad 'except:' catching the
SystemExit exception emitted by sys.exit(), but this would mask any
other exceptions and make debugging potential problem difficult.

This commit introduces an hopefully cleaner way to handle this case by
defining an user exception 'DBConfigNotFoundError' that is raised if the
db.ini file cannot be read.  This exception is ignored in the early
connection made in scripts/msnoise.py while looking up installed
plugins, as at this stage the file can legitimately not exist.  The
exception is however caught in the run() function of the same file to
present a clean error message to the user before exiting the program.

Better handling of a missing db.ini

As the db.ini is looked up through api.connect() very early at runtime,
even before any provided subcommand is even taken into account, db.ini
can legitimately not exist (as it is the case when running 'msnoise db
init').  api.read_database_inifile() should therefore not do a
sys.exit() when the file is not found, as an exit is not always wanted.

This was previously resolved by a very broad 'except:' catching the
SystemExit exception emitted by sys.exit(), but this would mask any
other exceptions and make debugging potential problem difficult.

This commit introduces an hopefully cleaner way to handle this case by
defining an user exception 'DBConfigNotFoundError' that is raised if the
db.ini file cannot be read.  This exception is ignored in the early
connection made in scripts/msnoise.py while looking up installed
plugins, as at this stage the file can legitimately not exist.  The
exception is however caught in the run() function of the same file to
present a clean error message to the user before exiting the program.

sram_factory: Give proper priority to overrides

modules overridden by the user are the highest priority, then modules
overridden by the technology. If nothing is overriden, use the defaults
from OPTS (if they exist) or use the requested module_type.

This fixes that custom tech_modules could not be used, if they had a default in
OPTS even if the latter was not overridden by the user.

We don't need extra defaults in the tech_modules, as we now only use them,
if they have been overridden by the tech_module.

port_data: Refactor channel_route/connect_bitlines()

both functions share a lot of code and are passing around a lot of data
under similar names (inst1, inst1_start_bit, inst1_bl_name, ...). Thus
we group all these elements in a named tuple to ease passing around
these elements.

All callers of channel_route/connect_bitlines() either pass in the bl/br
names or rely on "br_{}"/"bl_{}" as defaults. These hard coded values
should be determined by the instances. Thus we get the bitline names
based on the instances passed in. The callers only provide a template
string, to take care of the case that bitlines are called "bl_out_{}".

fix the types in --copy and --entrypoint (#500)

* fix the types in --copy and --entrypoint

Both of these options use the class OptionEatAll. By default, this class
will output a string type, but that would result in a string that looked
like a tuple. For example, it is possible to use `ast.literal_eval(value)`
on the value to convert it back to a tuple. To fix this, this commit
sets the type for --copy and --entrypoint to `tuple` and the subsequent
code expects the values for --copy and --entrypoint to be tuples.

This commit also adds a type hint to an OptionsEatAll internal to help
with debugging.

* expand issue 498 tests for --copy and --entrypoint

* change assertions to raise click.ClickException

This formats the error messages better (and with less clutter). This
commit also adds a note to contact the devs in the case of errors that
users cannot fix (errors in the implementation...).

* raise an error if OptionEatAll is used as a str type

The fundamental issue leading to #498 was that the values in
OptionEatAll were being coerced to a string type if no type was
specified in OptionEatAll. This made a tuple `('foo',)` into a string
`'("foo",)'`. This commit raises an error if OptionEatAll is used as a
string. Indeed, the 'eat-all' nature of this option suggests that there
are multiple options, which suggests the type should be a list or tuple.

This commit also adds a test for this.

raise an error if OptionEatAll is used as a str type

The fundamental issue leading to #498 was that the values in
OptionEatAll were being coerced to a string type if no type was
specified in OptionEatAll. This made a tuple `('foo',)` into a string
`'("foo",)'`. This commit raises an error if OptionEatAll is used as a
string. Indeed, the 'eat-all' nature of this option suggests that there
are multiple options, which suggests the type should be a list or tuple.

This commit also adds a test for this.

fix the types in --copy and --entrypoint

Both of these options use the class OptionEatAll. By default, this class
will output a string type, but that would result in a string that looked
like a tuple. For example, it is possible to use `ast.literal_eval(value)`
on the value to convert it back to a tuple. To fix this, this commit
sets the type for --copy and --entrypoint to `tuple` and the subsequent
code expects the values for --copy and --entrypoint to be tuples.

This commit also adds a type hint to an OptionsEatAll internal to help
with debugging.

upon different tools. Immediate use case - FSL 6.0.1

    $ DISPLAY=:0 fsl
    Error in startup script: can't read "env(USER)": no such variable
        while executing
    "set USER       $env(USER)"
        (file "/opt/fsl-6.0.1/tcl/fslstart.tcl" line 6)
        invoked from within
    "source [ file dirname [ info script ] ]/fslstart.tcl"
        (file "/opt/fsl-6.0.1/tcl/fsl.tcl" line 71)
        invoked from within
    "source ${FSLDIR}/tcl/${origname}.tcl"
        (file "/opt/fsl-6.0.1/bin/fsl" line 22)

but I thought it would generally be useful and should not have
side-effects, that is why added to the generic startup script.
The only concern I just got is reprozip minimized images -- would they
have whoami?  But even then, the situation should not be grave since
`whoami` seems to be not executed if USER is defined, so should generally
work ;)

of the git repository, and `git status` was reporting uncommitted
changes. This caused the command `neurodocker --version` to show that
there were uncommitted changes (by including the `dirty` suffix in the
version). We do not want users to be under the impression that the
version includes uncommitted changes. Indeed, kaczmarj excluded `/docs`
from the docker builds as a premature optimization... it turns out that
they only consume 136 kb, which is negligible.
